title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator Suite for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered, and executed a reproducible synthetic benchmark and a deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM configuration generator on operational intent→configuration tasks. The preregistered paired design used N=300 tasks across four intent categories (75 per cluster) and declared model gpt-5-mini; the deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). Outcomes were binary per task (validator pass/fail). Results: baseline (single‑pass) 299/300 passes, guarded (GVR) 300/300 passes; paired contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333333333332993; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Critically, provider_call_audit shows the guarded repair stage executed only once (shared_initial_generation = 300, repair = 1; total model_calls_used = 301), i.e., the GVR repair stage was rarely triggered under the chosen validator semantics and repair budget (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR materially increases pass rate (target effect 0.10 with planned ≈80% power at N=300) was not supported. We interpret the outcome as driven by a ceiling effect together with minimal GVR engagement, discuss construct and external validity limits, and provide the sealed preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, and analysis artifacts (included in the submission bundle) to enable community extension.

sections.introduction: Motivation. Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed to automate NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation and change planning. Prior work reports that naive LLM outputs can contain syntax, topology, or semantic errors and that combining generation with deterministic verifiers and iterative repair can reduce such errors. However, the field lacks a standardized, machine‑checkable benchmark that (i) couples synthetic yet operationally structured intent tasks with deterministic validator semantics, and (ii) supports sealed confirmatory comparisons of defended pipelines (GVR) versus single‑pass generation. Research question. Using a sealed paired preregistered design, can a standardized synthetic task set and deterministic validator reveal a material per‑task correctness advantage for an automated GVR pipeline over a frozen single‑pass LLM under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget? Contributions. (1) a publicly archived synthetic task generator and deterministic validator specification tuned to operational intent constraints; (2) a sealed preregistered paired experiment (ac-2026-003-prereg-v1) comparing a guarded GVR pipeline to single‑pass generation with gpt-5-mini on N=300 tasks; (3) a complete archival bundle (preregistration, execution manifest, raw outputs, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts) and an explicit articulation of why the observed near‑ceiling outcome, together with minimal GVR engagement, constrains confirmatory interpretation.
sections.related_work: Positioning. Surveys and reviews document rapid growth in LLM applications for NetOps and repeatedly highlight evaluation and realism gaps [Long et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024]. Technical studies show LLMs can synthesize router configurations but often require verifier assistance to avoid misconfigurations [Mondal et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2024]. Context‑aware iterative prompting and generate–validate–repair architectures can increase correction rates in focused evaluations [Jiang et al., 2024]. Security literature documents prompt injection and adversarial risks relevant to operational workflows [Shen et al., 2024]. These works motivate a sealed, artifact‑grounded confirmatory comparison using machine‑checkable correctness semantics rather than only language‑level metrics.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and primary hypothesis. We preregistered study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 (preregistration SHA‑256: a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765). Primary confirmatory hypothesis H1: the GVR pipeline yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass LLM on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). Design. Paired binary design: for each task a single shared initial generation candidate was produced (used as the baseline single‑pass candidate). The guarded condition executed the same initial generation and then ran a deterministic validator; if and only if the validator reported failure the guarded pipeline could perform up to one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This shared‑initial design controls generation variance and isolates repair effectiveness. Task bank and validator. A deterministic task generator produced 300 intent→configuration tasks across four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 tasks each). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, and workflow_policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, minimum_active_in_groups). The validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, v5.0) implements the scoring rule labeled "full_intent_constraint_validation" and emits a structured diagnostic and a binary score=1 with score_reason_code=VALID_CONFIGURATION when all declared constraints are satisfied. Validator behavior (parsing, normalization of semantically permitted ordering, enforcement of required_sequence and workflow_policies, preserve_unspecified_state semantics, and the fields emitted) is summarized in the manuscript and fully recorded per task in execution/scoring/*.json. Models and orchestration. Declared model: gpt-5-mini. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter implemented the baseline shared initial generation and the guarded GVR pipeline (generate→validator→at most one automated repair). Preregistered missingness, exclusions, and analysis. Exclusion rules removed ambiguous specifications or contamination; none occurred. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, tested with an exact McNemar two‑sided test on the paired binary outcomes; a paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) produced a percentile 95% CI. The run recorded seeds, provider traces, and all model/validator outputs in the archived bundle.
sections.results: Execution and accounting. The confirmatory run completed per the preregistered plan: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600 (300 shared initial generation calls used as the baseline candidate + up to 300 guarded repair attempts subject to the repair trigger policy), model_calls_used = 301, failed_episode_count = 0, complete_pair_count = 300. Critically, provider_call_audit and deterministic reconciliation record that stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and condition_counts = {shared: 300, guarded: 1}; thus the guarded repair stage executed only once across the N=300 tasks. Primary outcomes. Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (baseline_success_rate = 0.9966666666666667). Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). Paired contingency (guarded, baseline): n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 (the exact implementation tests symmetry of discordant pairs; with discordants n10=1 and n01=0 the two‑sided exact test yields p=1.0 given extreme imbalance and small counts). Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729): [0.00, 0.01]. Interpretation of statistical outcome. The observed discordant pattern (one guarded‑only success and zero baseline‑only successes) produces an exact McNemar p that does not reject symmetry; the single discordant observation and the very high baseline rate mean the test is underpowered to detect small differences and that the bootstrap CI includes 0, consistent with a negligible observed paired difference. Representative artifacts. Representative per‑task scoring artifacts and shared initial responses are archived under execution/scoring/*.json and execution/responses/*.txt (examples included in the submission bundle). Analysis artifacts (analysis/condition_summary.csv and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) contain the aggregated counts used for inference.
sections.discussion: What the run shows and what it does not. The preregistered paired experiment and archived artifacts demonstrate that under the chosen synthetic task set, snapshot validator semantics, and a constrained repair budget (≤1 repair call per task), baseline single‑pass generation already satisfied validator constraints on nearly all tasks (299/300), leaving little headroom for an automated repair policy to improve observable pass rates. Two interlocking factors constrain confirmatory inference: (1) ceiling effect: baseline success ≈99.7% yields minimal room for improvement relative to the preregistered target effect (0.10), and (2) GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage was triggered only once (repair stage_counts = 1), so the comparison was effectively between identical initial candidates rather than an actively repaired set in most tasks. These facts are recorded in the execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json), deterministic_reconciliation.json, and provider_call_audit in the archived bundle. Methodological implications. The result is a valid negative/ceiling observation for the particular benchmark‑validator‑repair budget combination: it does not imply GVR lacks value generally. Different repair trigger policies, larger repair budgets (multiple iterative repairs), alternative validator constructs (stateful temporal simulation or emulation rather than snapshot checks), increased task difficulty, or multi‑model comparisons could increase GVR engagement and sensitivity to method differences. Statistical note. The exact McNemar p=1.0 arises from the small and imbalanced discordant counts (n10=1, n01=0) and should be interpreted in that light: it indicates no evidence of asymmetric success behavior favoring one condition given the observed discordants, but it does not imply evidence of equivalence in broader operational conditions. Limitations and external validity. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot, task‑declared workflow_policies and required sequences but does not model temporal in‑flight dynamics, vendor idiosyncrasies, or runtime side effects. Tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity. Only gpt-5-mini was evaluated. Reproducibility and artifact access. The full preregistration, execution manifest, raw results, per‑task validator traces, model configuration, and analysis artifacts are included in the submission bundle (authoritative paths inside the bundle include: execution/execution_manifest.json, execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, execution/scoring/*.json, execution/responses/*.txt, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv). These archive files are the authoritative provenance for all empirical claims in this paper.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a reproducible synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator suite and ran a sealed paired confirmatory comparison of a GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both methods achieved near‑perfect validator pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR materially improves pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported on this task set. Importantly, the guarded repair stage executed only once (repair stage_counts = 1), so the experiment largely compared identical shared initial candidates rather than actively repaired outputs. We release the task generator, deterministic validator specification, raw outputs, and analysis artifacts to enable community extensions (harder tasks, stateful validators, different repair budgets, multi‑model evaluations) that can better reveal where GVR pipelines provide measurable operational value.

limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot, task‑declared workflow_policies and required sequences but does not model temporal in‑flight dynamics, vendor execution idiosyncrasies, or traffic/performance impacts.

External validity: synthetic tasks (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) do not capture full production heterogeneity; results do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) limit sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain the confirmatory inference regarding practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further multi‑model experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving planned exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing exact hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider conditions recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the execution manifest.
